qt: to the Commission Bruno Gonçalves (S&D) Subject:

As a consequence of recent international developments, security of energy supply has regained a central role in public policy. This is substantiated, inter alia, by the decision of NATO partners to set 1.5 % of GDP as a target for investment in critical infrastructure. Against this backdrop, the Portuguese Government has announced the acquisition of a 13.7 % stake in REN (the company responsible for the electricity and gas grids in mainland Portugal). This position raises the following questions, also in relation to the competences of the European Commission in this area: 1.
What view does the Commission take of public control in transmission system operators (TSOs) with regard to the EU priority of energy security?
Does it think EU sovereignty is more secure if Member States have majority stakes in these operators?
Thank you for shedding light on this matter.
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.10.2026) The EU internal energy market framework (Regulation (EU) 2019/9431, Directive (EU) 2019/9442) defines requirements on unbundling, independence, non-discrimination, network planning, investment obligations and security and reliability of network operation. Provided that the applicable EU law is fully respected, the ownership model of transmission system operators (TSOs) is a matter for the Member States and the undertakings concerned. The Electricity Directive 2019/944 sets out unbundling requirements for electricity TSOs to ensure that decision making of the TSO is independent from any interests in generation and supply activities (Article 43.1(b)). Article 43.5 allows Member States or public bodies to exercise control or any right in a TSO and an undertaking performing functions of generation or supply only under the condition that these rights are exercised through two separate public bodies. For energy security, the ability of the operator to ensure the safe, reliable and efficient functioning of the transmission system, including adequate investment, resilience and crossborder cooperation, is a key consideration. Ownership is also an important criterion for security of supply. Regulation (EU) 2019/9413 requires risk assessments to consider risks linked to the ownership of infrastructures relevant for security of electricity supply. The Commission’s approach is to ensure that all TSOs operating in the EU, irrespective of their ownership model, fully comply with EU rules and contribute to the EU’s objectives of energy security, market integration and decarbonisation.
